dek.text: A Montgomery County court struck a deposition transcript made with AI because no certified reporter prepared it. The Supreme Court of Texas heard the dispute and has not ruled.

introduction.text: [The Supreme Court of Texas heard argument over whether a party should be allowed to submit a deposition transcript generated with AI as evidence, Courthouse News reports](c6). [The court listed the case, In re Patrick Hughey, on its submission schedule for {{date:c23}} as a petition for writ of mandamus from Montgomery County and the Ninth District](c23).

[The case began as a Montgomery County man's wrongful termination claim against his former employer](c7). The fight in front of the court is narrower. It is about who has to stand behind the written record of what a witness said.

paragraphs.text: [The employer did not object to the transcription software at the deposition. It asked the trial court to strike the transcript several weeks later](c10). [The trial court struck it from the record because no certified shorthand reporter prepared it](c8).

[The Ninth District Court of Appeals denied the employee in an unsigned ruling, Courthouse News reports, and found the issue was the uncertified written transcript rather than the content of the deposition or its use as evidence](c9).

[The Texas Rules of Civil Procedure let any party have an oral deposition recorded by other than stenographic means, including on video](c26). [The party asking for that kind of recording must obtain a person authorized to administer the oath and assure the recording will be intelligible, accurate and trustworthy](c27).

[A written transcription of such a recording may be used to the same extent as a deposition taken by stenographic means](c28). [A court may still require a complete transcript from a certified court reporter first, on good cause shown](c29). Whether the transcript in this case falls inside that allowance is the question the court has taken up.

[Bradley Snead argued for the employee that the deposition's video recording is certified, so the transcript does not have to be](c13). [He told the court it can write more rules if it wants and said the current rules allow what his client did](c14).

[Stephanie L. Bryant argued for the employer that depositions transcribed this cheaply by AI programs would multiply discovery costs](c15). [She said she had no issue with lawyers using their own in-house AI software, and argued that a third-party platform like the one the employee used raises security and confidentiality questions](c16). [The Texas Deposition Reporters Association shared her side's time as amicus curiae](c25), [and the court reporters' trade association filed its own amicus brief](c3).

[Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock observed that paying a certified reporter, or letting the depositions go ahead this way, would have been cheaper, and asked "Why are we here?"](c11) [Justice Kyle Hawkins said the other side can point out an error and watch the video](c18), [and asked why the court should set aside what he called an efficient, cost-effective tool](c19).

[Justice Jane Bland asked where the court would find the assurance of a human being standing behind the transcribed product](c12). [Justice J. Brett Busby asked whether the court's proportionality rules would answer the concern about cost](c17). [Justice Evan Young said the court has escape hatches, naming the recording itself and a judge's power to order a certified shorthand reporter](c20).

[Courthouse News read the argument as showing the justices inclined to allow AI transcripts where verified video recordings serve as the check. That is the outlet's reading, and the court has not ruled](c21). [Justice John Devine was absent from the argument](c22).

A ruling would say whether a video recording can stand behind a transcript no certified reporter prepared. It would also say what a trial judge should treat as good cause to demand one. Until the court decides, the trial court's order striking the transcript is the last word in this case.
